lesson.title: Giving Reasons to Support Your Opinion
lesson.subject: ela

contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you wrote a clear opinion. Today let's make it convincing by adding real reasons — the 'why' behind your belief.

A strong opinion has at least two or three reasons backing it up. Take the opinion: 'Students should have a class pet.' Reasons might be: it teaches responsibility, it can reduce stress, and it helps students learn about animals. Notice each reason is a real, specific point — not just repeating the opinion in different words. Try writing two reasons for your own opinion from yesterday.
Reasons are what turn an opinion into an argument someone might actually agree with. Tomorrow we'll learn how to organize your opinion and reasons into a real paragraph.

objectives: Write at least two specific, distinct reasons that support a given opinion
Distinguish a real reason from a restatement of the opinion itself
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Present the class-pet opinion and brainstorm reasons together.
2. Point out the difference between a real reason and just repeating the opinion.
3. Practice writing 2-3 reasons for one more shared opinion.
4. Move to the worksheet: write two reasons for the opinion statement from yesterday.
5. Close by reading the opinion plus reasons together as a mini-argument.
differentiationTips: Struggling: brainstorm reasons together out loud before asking the child to write them independently
Ready for more: ask the child to rank their reasons from strongest to weakest and explain why
For a child who enjoys debate, have them think of a counter-argument and then explain why their reason still holds up
teacherGuide.answerKey: Open-ended — check that each reason is specific and distinct, not simply a restatement of the opinion.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Supporting an opinion with real reasons is a core Grade 3 opinion-writing standard (matching Common Core W.3.1b), directly building on yesterday's opinion-statement lesson.
